title: The Promises and Pitfalls of Personalisation
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen asks when AI-driven personalised examples help learning and when they quietly break the concept being taught, drawing on three education theorists to build a practical framework. From Ference Marton's Variation Theory, she takes the principle that examples must vary the surface while keeping the concept's critical, invariant feature constant. From Karl Maton's Legitimation Code Theory, she takes "semantic gravity" -- whether an idea's meaning travels safely across contexts (weak gravity, e.g. finding a mean) or is tightly bound to context (strong gravity, e.g. judging a historical source's credibility). From Samuel Messick's validity theory, she takes the warning against "construct-irrelevant variance" -- personalised details that inadvertently change what is actually being assessed or taught. She applies this framework to Google's "Learn Your Way" personalisation tool across three real examples (data structures via cooking, economic systems via football, human evolution via photography), finding personalisation works well for concepts with weak semantic gravity and clean binary correctness, but actively risks distorting concepts, like natural selection, where context is doing real explanatory work.
points: Allen's three-theorist framework (Marton's invariants, Maton's semantic gravity, Messick's construct-irrelevant variance) turns a vague intuition -- "does this example help or hurt?" -- into a checkable set of questions any teacher or AI-tool designer can apply.

Her football/economic-systems case study catches a subtle but consequential error in Google's tool: presenting a youth academy as an example of a "command economy" collapses organisational hierarchy into economic system, teaching a rule that will actively mislead students later.

The evolution/photography case is her strongest cautionary example -- a camera-technology analogy for evolution smuggles in goal-directed design and teleology, priming exactly the misconception ("things evolve to get better") that biology teachers spend years correcting.

Allen's closing reframe is important: personalisation isn't inherently good or bad, it's a design choice that either amplifies the signal (when semantic gravity is weak and the construct is clean) or buries it (when context is part of the thing being taught).
quotes: Imagine if I’d learnt statistics solely through examples from music and politics. Would I have loved it sooner? The question matters now because AI promises personalised tutors that connect dry subjects to students’ real interests.
Understanding comes from seeing the critical feature come into relief through contrast, and then, once discerned, seeing it persist as non-critical features vary.

When gravity is weak (abstract ideas), knowledge tends to travel well across different stories or settings; when gravity is strong (context does the work), changing the setting can quietly change the thing being learned.
An academy is a private organisation inside a market/mixed system. Internal top-down management is not equal to society-wide central planning.
Cameras don’t reproduce; lineages do. As framed, the example is memorable but mechanistically wrong, so it primes exactly the misconceptions we’re trying to avoid.
Personalisation isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a menace. It’s a design choice that either amplifies the signal or buries it.
